newsitem.title: USA: Netanyahu gives little in White House summit.
newsitem.headline: Netanyahu gives little in White House summit.

text.p: Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu looked and talked like a man who got everything he wanted and gave up nothing when a White House summit ended on Wednesday.
With good reason, said the Palestinians.
The Palestinian peace partners he inherited with his election 15 weeks ago felt the losers.

The summit, called to quell an outburst of violence, featured only the second meeting between the Israeli leader and Yasir Arafat, the Palestinian president who only a few months ago Netanyahu dismissed as the head of a terrorist organisation.
Netanyahu ceded nothing in the two days of talks. None of the differences that boiled over into violence was resolved.

The only agreements reached were to accept the two proposals the hardline prime minister had offered on his plane to Washington -- a commitment to end the violence and launch intensive negotiations beginning next week on an Israeli pullback from the West Bank city of Hebron, the one main subject of Israeli-PLO peace deals yet to be implemented.
By agreeing to intensify negotiations, Netanyahu was only agreeing to something that had already been done.
Palestinians already have a detailed deal on Hebron with the Jewish state. It was signed a year ago by Israel and the PLO in the presence of President Bill Clinton.
Clinton, at a news conference ending the summit, tried to say that the new negotiatons would focus on "implementation," of the Hebron deal. He insisted this was different from a renegotiation.

Netanyahu hopes that by reopening the Hebron accord he can boast to Israelis that he clinched a better deal for the 400 Jews living there surrounded by 100,000 Arabs than did his Nobel Peace Laureate predecessors Yitzhak Rabin and Shimon Peres.

Netanyahu further managed to resist U.S. pressure that he commit to a date for pulling back from the occupied city. A senior Israeli official said it could take "weeks" but called that likelihood "iffy" at best.

Palestinians said the peace process, which Clinton had nurtured since its inception three years ago, was on the verge of collapse. Arafat did not show up for a post-summit news conference he had planned to hold.
"The peace process is on the verge of collapse," said Mustafa Natsheh, mayor of Hebron.
In the Israeli camp by contrast, the mood was upbeat.
"The results of the summit are a great success from the point of view of the government of Israel," Cabinet Secretary Danny Naveh said.

Netanyahu, trying not to appear smug at the outcome, stressed the talks had been useful because Israel refused to make concessions under pressure. "Very, very bad things didn't happen while we were here," he said.

Israel was not forced to close the tourist tunnel built near a Moslem holy site, the opening of which evoked Palestinian rage pent up over Netanyahu's slowing of the pace of peace negotiations, Israeli officials said.
By getting both sides to agree to shun violence, Netanyahu could claim victory for an Israeli public that elected him on a promise to boost security.
Netanyahu insisted he and Arafat achieved greater understanding. An Israeli official said their meeting was "pleasant" this time than a much shorter one last month at their border.

Then two teams of negotiators met on opposite sides of a long table, the official said. This time the two leaders sat each with an aide at his side over chicken and couscous for three hours in the White House library.
Netanyahu said the two sides must learn to establish trust. But Palestinians, looking for negotiations built on give and take, were wondering this time what they got.
